We study the tail-overlap interaction of a well-separated pair of dissipative solitons in systems with slow saturable gain. Gain saturation introduces nonlocal terms in the soliton field equation that depend on the total energy and therefore invalidate the standard methods used to study overlap inte…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014205] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the interaction of dissipative solitons in systems with saturable gain, focusing on tail-overlap effects.
motivation: Understanding soliton interactions is important for applications in nonlinear optics and laser physics, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model incorporating nonlocal terms due to gain saturation and analyze the interaction dynamics.
result: They find that gain saturation introduces new interaction regimes not captured by standard methods.
conclusion: The work contributes to nonlinear wave theory but has no relevance to the specified research interests.

title: Segregation Dynamics In Active-passive Mixtures Of Semiflexible Filaments
authors: Chitrak Bhowmik, Aparna Baskaran, And Sriram Ramaswamy
abstract:
Author(s): Chitrak Bhowmik, Aparna Baskaran, and Sriram Ramaswamy

We study the segregation of motile semiflexible filaments from a background of similar but nonmotile filaments. Our Langevin dynamics simulations reveal a wide range of emergent structures governed by filament flexibility and activity, i.e., self-propulsion strength. The system segregates at low act…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 015405] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies segregation dynamics in active-passive mixtures of semiflexible filaments using Langevin dynamics simulations.
motivation: Understanding how active and passive filaments segregate is important for biological and soft matter systems, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Langevin dynamics simulations of semiflexible filaments with varying flexibility and activity.
result: The system exhibits a wide range of emergent structures depending on filament flexibility and activity, with segregation occurring at low activity.
conclusion: Filament flexibility and activity govern the segregation behavior, but the work is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Phase-symmetry Breaking As A Mechanism For Subcritical Transition In Shell Models Of Turbulence
authors: Yoshiki Hiruta
abstract:
Author(s): Yoshiki Hiruta

Subcritical transition to turbulence, in which the laminar state is linearly stable yet finite-amplitude perturbations develop into turbulence, is ubiquitous but predicting it from the structure of the governing equations remains difficult. We demonstrate such a framework using a shell model of turb…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, L013101] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies subcritical transition to turbulence in a shell model of turbulence, focusing on phase-symmetry breaking as a mechanism.
motivation: Predicting subcritical transition to turbulence from the structure of governing equations is difficult; the paper aims to demonstrate a framework using a shell model.
method: The authors analyze a shell model of turbulence and investigate the role of phase-symmetry breaking in triggering subcritical transition.
result: They show that phase-symmetry breaking can lead to subcritical transition in the shell model.
conclusion: The work provides insight into the mechanism of subcritical turbulence but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Short Peptide-grafted Interfaces Regulate Protein Cluster Coacervation
authors: Chen-Yang Fan, Chun-Lai Ren, And Yu-Qiang Ma
abstract:
Author(s): Chen-yang Fan, Chun-lai Ren, and Yu-qiang Ma

The behavior of protein condensates driven by weak multivalent interactions has been extensively studied in bulk systems, yet their interfacial behavior remains far less explored. Using coarse-grained simulations, we investigated protein clusters adsorbed onto interfaces grafted with short peptides …


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 015404] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies protein cluster coacervation on peptide-grafted interfaces using coarse-grained simulations.
motivation: Understanding interfacial behavior of protein condensates is important for cellular organization but remains poorly understood.
method: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of protein clusters adsorbed onto interfaces grafted with short peptides.
result: The grafted peptides modulate cluster morphology and dynamics, leading to distinct coacervation regimes.
conclusion: Interfacial grafting provides a means to control protein condensate behavior, with implications for biomaterials and cellular biology.

title: Shear Jamming Transition In Alternating Shear Rotation For Frictional And Frictionless Suspensions
authors: Pappu Acharya And Martin Trulsson
abstract:
Author(s): Pappu Acharya and Martin Trulsson

Alternating shear rotations in dense suspensions have recently shown the ability to reduce both viscosity and dissipation per strain (at a fixed global shear rate). Here, we study alternating shear rotations, with extensive numerical simulations, at various angles and up to their corresponding jammi…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033013] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies shear jamming transitions in dense suspensions under alternating shear rotations, focusing on rheological properties.
motivation: Understanding jamming transitions in suspensions is important for material science, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors perform extensive numerical simulations of frictional and frictionless suspensions under alternating shear rotations at various angles.
result: They observe a shear jamming transition and characterize how alternating shear reduces viscosity and dissipation.
conclusion: The findings are relevant to soft matter physics but have no direct application to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Stretched-exponential Aging Governs Nonequilibrium Precipitate Patterns
authors: Amari Z. Morris And Oliver Steinbock
abstract:
Author(s): Amari Z. Morris and Oliver Steinbock

Localized growth in driven materials is often governed by intermittent failure, yet how a material's history biases failure sites remains poorly understood. Using pause-restart experiments on chemical precipitate membranes, we quantify the probability of age-dependent breaching. We show that the kin…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033025] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies aging and breaching in chemical precipitate membranes, a non-equilibrium pattern formation problem.
motivation: Understanding how material history biases failure sites in driven materials is poorly understood.
method: Pause-restart experiments on chemical precipitate membranes quantify the probability of age-dependent breaching.
result: Stretched-exponential aging governs the nonequilibrium precipitate patterns.
conclusion: The findings provide insight into intermittent failure in driven materials.

title: Focusing Characteristics Of Cylindrically Bent Laue Crystals
authors: Yu-Hang Wang, Ming Li, And Quan-Jie Jia
abstract:

result: They obtain monochromatic and polychromatic focusing conditions and a conservation relation describing aperture effects.
conclusion: The framework offers a comprehensive description of focusing in cylindrically bent Laue crystals, useful for X-ray optics design.

authors: J. von der Linden, A. Deller, S. Nißl, K. Michishio, H. Higaki, And E. V. Stenson

title: Hydrodynamic Attraction And Hindered Diffusion Govern First-passage Times Of Swimming Microorganisms
authors: Yanis Baouche, Magali Le Goff, Thomas Franosch, And Christina Kurzthaler
abstract:
Author(s): Yanis Baouche, Magali Le Goff, Thomas Franosch, and Christina Kurzthaler

Numerical simulations of force-dipole microswimmers near a no-slip wall reveal how hydrodynamic interactions and diffusion shape first-passage-time statistics. The results show that wall-induced hindered diffusion can strongly delay wall encounters, while active hydrodynamic attraction produces distinct behaviors for pushers and pullers, including a nonmonotonic dependence on dipole strength.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022060] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies first-passage times of swimming microorganisms near a wall using numerical simulations, focusing on hydrodynamic attraction and hindered diffusion.
motivation: Understanding how microorganisms navigate near surfaces is important for biological and ecological processes, but the role of hydrodynamic interactions and diffusion on first-passage times is not well understood.
method: Numerical simulations of force-dipole microswimmers near a no-slip wall are performed to compute first-passage-time statistics.
result: Wall-induced hindered diffusion delays wall encounters, while active hydrodynamic attraction leads to distinct behaviors for pushers and pullers, including a nonmonotonic dependence on dipole strength.
conclusion: Hydrodynamic interactions and diffusion significantly affect the first-passage times of swimming microorganisms near walls, with implications for microbial ecology and biophysics.

authors: I. Festi, E. Alfinelli, D. Bessas, F. Caporaletti, A. I. Chumakov, M. Moratalla, M. A. Ramos, M. Rodríguez-López, C. Rodríguez-Tinoco, J. Rodríguez-Viejo, And G. Baldi

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the interplay of surface defects, electric fields, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation and evolution.
result: A unified model emerges where tiny surface protrusions, field emission, Joule heating, and ion bombardment lead to runaway plasma formation.
conclusion: Recent advances provide a clear physical understanding of vacuum breakdown, which can guide the design of more robust accelerator structures and other high-voltage vacuum systems.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review unifies the description of radiation forces and torques in optical and acoustic fields, focusing on momentum and spin densities.
motivation: Understanding how wave fields exert forces and torques on particles is fundamental for applications like optical trapping and acoustic manipulation.
method: The authors present a unified theoretical framework based on local energy, momentum, and spin densities in both optical and acoustic wave fields.
result: They show that the same physical principles govern radiation forces and torques in optics and acoustics, enabling cross-disciplinary insights.
conclusion: The unified perspective can guide future developments in particle manipulation using light and sound.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and the multimessenger implications for astrophysics.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper reviews detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and emphasizes simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It surveys potential implications for understanding physical and astrophysical processes in dense neutron star environments.
conclusion: Multimessenger observations with continuous gravitational waves will enhance our understanding of neutron star interiors and related physics.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars.
method: Review of gravitational-wave and X-ray observations, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are summarized.
conclusion: Future observations will further constrain the dense matter equation of state.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, but recent experimental results have constrained its parameter space. The paper aims to survey the current status and future discovery potential.
method: The authors review theoretical models and experimental search strategies, and project discovery potential for the HL-LHC across multiple channels.
result: The paper provides an overview of viable supersymmetric scenarios and their expected signatures at the HL-LHC.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains a compelling framework, and the HL-LHC will significantly extend the search sensitivity.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion and neutrino production.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The review summarizes theoretical and experimental advances in nuclear reaction rates, plasma physics, and solar modeling.
result: It presents updated nuclear reaction data and improved solar models that better match observations.
conclusion: The work advances astrophysical understanding but has no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers three real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper aims to review techniques that provide direct real-space access.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined approaches.
result: The review highlights how these techniques can characterize disorder and defects in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy methods are powerful for understanding atomic-scale disorder, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonances.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions at stellar energies is crucial for stellar burning and nucleosynthesis, but many reactions are difficult to measure directly.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques for studying these reactions.
result: It provides a comprehensive overview of current theoretical and experimental methods for low-energy nuclear astrophysics.
conclusion: The review highlights the importance of quantum phenomena in stellar nuclear reactions and outlines future directions for research.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022

motivation: Accurate and consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology, and periodic updates are needed as new measurements become available.
method: A least-squares adjustment is performed on a carefully selected set of experimental data and theoretical calculations to produce self-consistent values with uncertainties.
result: The 2022 set of recommended values for fundamental constants and conversion factors is provided, along with their uncertainties.
conclusion: The CODATA recommended values serve as the internationally accepted standard for fundamental constants, supporting research and applications across physics and chemistry.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed for biological and clinical insight; optoacoustic imaging offers high-resolution, deep-tissue optical contrast noninvasively.
method: The review discusses the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: The paper summarizes the state of the art in optoacoustic microscopy and its applications.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological imaging, but the paper does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

motivation: Stellarators have inherent steady-state capability and lack disruptions, but historically lag behind tokamaks in triple product performance. The goal is to demonstrate that optimized stellarators can reach tokamak-level confinement.
method: Experiments on the Wendelstein 7-X stellarator were conducted to achieve and maintain peaked density profiles, and the triple product was measured and compared to tokamak performance.

motivation: Understanding the small-scale statistics of turbulent flows is important for many physical systems, and the role of dilatation in compressible turbulence is not well understood.
method: The authors perform direct numerical simulations of three-dimensional isothermal compressible homogeneous isotropic turbulence and analyze moments of energy dissipation and its components.
result: They identify a transition to a dilatation-dominated regime where the dilatational component of dissipation becomes dominant over the solenoidal component.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into the energy dissipation mechanisms in compressible turbulence, which may have implications for astrophysical and engineering flows.

We derive a general criterion fo…

method: The authors derive a general criterion for stable concentration-based size control using a mathematical model.
result: They identify conditions under which concentration thresholds can robustly trigger cell division.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for understanding size control mechanisms in biology.

result: They find that octupole collectivity leaves distinct imprints on flow harmonics, which could be used to probe nuclear shapes.
conclusion: Heavy-ion collisions can serve as a tool to study nuclear structure, particularly octupole deformation in uranium-238.

result: Super-resonance enables broadband flow stabilization and other applications, breaking the traditional bandwidth limit.
conclusion: Super-resonance offers a new paradigm for resonant systems, with potential applications in flow control and beyond.

authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy emission from the Galactic Center, covering the supermassive black hole, compact sources, and plasma bubbles.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of the Galactic Center's high-energy phenomena.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of the Galactic Center's high-energy emission.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: Searching for new hadrons and understanding charmonium decays provides insights into QCD, quark confinement, and gluon binding.
method: The paper reviews experimental results from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments on hadron production in e+e- collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs.
result: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for high-precision measurements in this area, with recent advances highlighted.
conclusion: The review summarizes current progress and emphasizes the importance of these measurements for validating QCD and discovering new hadronic states.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the scientific legacy of planetary radar observations at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids.
result: Arecibo's radar system was the most sensitive of its kind, enabling detailed characterization of many Solar System objects.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system made significant contributions to planetary science, and its loss marks the end of an era.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the historical legacy and scientific contributions of the Arecibo 305-m radio telescope in radio astronomy.
motivation: To provide a historical perspective on Arecibo's impact across diverse astronomical fields, emphasizing its upgrades and discoveries.
method: The paper is a review, summarizing key scientific results from Arecibo's operations, including pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave background detection.
result: Arecibo made influential contributions to pulsar astronomy, neutral hydrogen mapping, interstellar medium characterization, VLBI imaging, SETI, and gravitational-wave astronomy.
conclusion: Arecibo's legacy in radio astronomy is enduring, with its upgrades enabling continuous expansion of observational capabilities and scientific breakthroughs.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews geospace science advances using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere have enabled significant advances in geospace science, and this Colloquium aims to summarize key results.
method: The paper reviews the incoherent scatter radar technique and presents findings from Arecibo's suite of instruments, including lidars and optical sensors, applied to ionospheric and magnetospheric studies.
result: Key advances in plasma physics, space weather, atomic metal layers, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling are highlighted.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in geospace research, and its legacy continues to inform upper atmospheric science.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The authors review experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of convection-cloud chambers that reproduce key cloud phenomena under controlled conditions.
result: Convection-cloud chambers provide insights into turbulent fluctuations and supersaturation that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to address the precipitation bottleneck, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection methods.
motivation: Observing a Galactic core collapse supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, providing insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.
method: The paper summarizes progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection and parameter estimation methods for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the latest modeling results and signal predictions, but does not introduce new results.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from supernovae is a key multimessenger strategy, but the paper is a review of astrophysical modeling and detection, not directly related to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on large-scale structure surveys.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole anisotropy in the distribution of radio galaxies and quasars with the cosmic microwave background dipole.
method: Analysis of large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in their distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may challenge the standard ΛCDM model, but further investigation of systematic effects is needed.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: A review of astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their observable signatures.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and test beyond-standard-model physics through astrophysical observations.
method: Review of theoretical predictions for self-interacting dark matter halos and comparison with observations from galaxies to large-scale structures.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross sections from various astrophysical probes.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable candidate, with ongoing and future observations expected to tighten constraints.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding bubble dynamics is important for many natural and industrial processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review summarizes experimental and theoretical advances over the past 20 years, focusing on fluid mechanics.
result: Key findings include the effects of added mass, deformable surfaces, turbulence, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The review provides insights for modeling two-phase flows but has no relevance to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.

tldr: This paper reviews nonlinear elasticity theory applied to buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding morphological instabilities in soft materials is important for materials science and biology, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.
